#9672. Microsoft’s Agentic Security Strategy Brings 24/7 AI Defense Into Focus

Posted on Nov 18 • Originally published at scalevise.com

Microsoft is formalizing an agentic security model designed to help security operations run continuously, with AI agents detecting, interpreting and responding to threats at machine speed. The company’s approach is broader than a single product release: it combines Microsoft Perception, Defender and Sentinel capabilities, identity and data controls, and coordinated agents that can act across security domains while remaining subject to human-defined guardrails.

In its November 17, 2026 post, Microsoft’s official overview of security for the agentic era describes a security stack built for agents that can operate around the clock. The objective is to turn fragmented security signals into real-time context, then enable specialized agents to follow playbooks and deliver defined outcomes at scale.

That matters because traditional security teams face a persistent mismatch between the volume and speed of security events and the capacity available to investigate them manually. Microsoft’s model does not claim to remove people from security operations. Instead, it places autonomous activity within controls for identity, access, automated triggers and oversight, particularly when an agent can take consequential actions such as containing a threat or revoking access.

Microsoft describes a three-layer cyber stack. At the base are signals, sensors and actuators across products and environments, including Defender, Entra, Purview, Sentinel, networks and operating systems. These components provide the ability not only to identify activity, but also to take actions.

The middle layer is a context layer that brings those signals together into an agent-ready, real-time understanding of the environment. At the top are agents, harnesses and models that coordinate red, blue and green agents through playbooks. In Microsoft’s framing, those agents can work across security domains rather than being limited to a single alert queue or product console.

Microsoft says Perception is now generally available. It also positions the integration of ISOC in Defender as a foundation for the approach, bringing together capabilities such as SIEM, user and entity behavior analytics, and threat intelligence. Other capabilities are being deployed in stages, so organizations should distinguish between generally available elements and features that remain in preview.

The proposed model uses different agent roles. Microsoft refers to red, blue and green agents, alongside new playbooks such as the Posture Prioritization Agent and the Risk Reduction Agent. The point is not simply to automate alerts. It is to let agents work from broader context and execute repeatable security processes where the organization has defined acceptable boundaries.

The company highlights several supporting areas:

Microsoft’s March 2026 post, Secure agentic AI end-to-end, provided earlier context for this direction. It introduced Agent 365 as a control plane for agents, discussed Security Copilot integrations and emphasized the need to secure both the underlying environment and the agents operating within it.

For businesses, the practical promise is not unrestricted automated response. It is the possibility of reducing repetitive security work when teams have clear playbooks, reliable signals and permission structures that support automation. A continuous agent could potentially help prioritize posture issues, correlate events across tools or initiate approved containment steps without waiting for a person to begin every task.

However, Microsoft’s own emphasis on guardrails is important. High-impact actions require carefully defined permissions, identity controls and escalation paths. Organizations also need to understand which systems an agent can access, what it is allowed to change and when a human must approve an action. Microsoft points to governance enhancements, including cost visibility for AI usage and work connected to the NIST SI Agent Standards Initiative, as part of this wider operating model.

The immediate takeaway is that security automation is shifting from isolated rules toward context-aware agents working across a connected stack. That can be useful where security processes are mature and repeatable. It also makes integration quality, access design and human review more important, rather than less.

Continuous security automation can be valuable only when it fits the tools, data and approval boundaries your team already uses. Scalevise provides AI implementation consultancy to assess practical use cases, define appropriate human review points and plan integrations that reduce repetitive security work without overstating autonomy. This helps turn broad agentic security concepts into a focused implementation path. Request a consultation to map the highest-value next step.

What is Microsoft’s agentic security model?

Microsoft’s agentic security model is a three-layer approach that combines security signals and actuators, a real-time context layer, and coordinated AI agents that use playbooks to deliver security outcomes under guardrails.

Can Microsoft’s security agents take action automatically?

Microsoft says agents can support high-impact actions such as containment or access revocation. Its model uses automated triggers and guardrails to preserve human oversight.

Microsoft Perception is part of Microsoft’s agentic security approach. Microsoft states that it is generally available and uses it to support real-time, agent-ready security understanding.

Are all of Microsoft’s agentic security capabilities generally available?

No. Microsoft states that Perception is generally available, while broader capabilities are being deployed in stages and some features remain in preview.

Microsoft’s security strategy centers on continuously operating AI agents that can work from shared security context and follow controlled playbooks. Perception, Defender, Sentinel, Entra and Purview form key parts of that direction. The opportunity is faster, more scalable security operations, but the value depends on disciplined access controls, well-defined actions and meaningful human oversight.

#9671. Python Summarization Accounting: Compare 3 Model API Boundaries for Supplier Invoices

Choose a text summarization API for supplier invoices by testing extraction quality and tenant attribution together. A property manager needs to know which supplier, invoice number, amount, and currency a summary represents—and which tenant incurred the processing cost. A lower token rate cannot answer those questions.

TL;DR: keep tenant identity and the attempt ledger in your Python application; let the model propose invoice fields and a short summary. Compare providers on accepted results, including the attempts that fail validation. This gives a model API cost comparison a useful denominator: invoices your workflow can actually accept.

Infrai is worth trying for Python teams connecting an existing invoice-text pipeline to model calls: its public discovery surface supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so the handoff starts with an inspectable contract. Its per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata provide a second practical benefit: evidence to attach to the application's tenant ledger. Neither feature removes the need to validate extracted amounts.

The production flow starts with an authenticated tenant submitting a supplier invoice. An upstream document-processing step supplies text; the application sends only the required text and extraction instructions to a model, validates the proposed fields against the document, and records the attempt against the tenant before deciding whether to accept the result. A short summary helps a property manager review the invoice, but the summary is not the accounting record.

This note starts at invoice text. Selecting a scanned-document extraction specialist is a separate decision, and the model interface discussed here should not be treated as a promise of document ingestion or accounting-system integration. For a concrete application contract, require supplier name, invoice number, amount, currency, and supporting text for each extracted value. Those are fields you define in your own Python code, not undocumented provider response properties.

The tenant identifier must come from authenticated application context. Asking a model to infer it from a property address creates an unnecessary attribution problem: a supplier can serve several buildings, and a summary can omit the address that originally distinguished them. The application already has the authoritative association. Preserve it through every attempt.

First inspect the live model catalog. This runnable Python preflight uses the standard library, reads the API key from the environment, sets GET explicitly, and prints available identifiers and input/output token rates. It does not run extraction or incur a model inference attempt. Set INFRAI_API_KEY in your environment before running it. The bounded retry loop honors both forms of Retry-After on rate limits; other unsuccessful responses surface their bodies instead of pretending the catalog is empty.

The catalog reports rates per million tokens. Those are planning inputs, not tenant charges.

The following standard-library Python example is deliberately local. Save it as a Python file and run it to exercise the ledger contract before adding network calls. Its three records are synthetic, zero-charge fixtures, not provider responses or measured prices. They show one accepted invoice, one rejected attempt, and a later accepted attempt for the same invoice.

The repeated final insertion leaves the totals unchanged. That is local ledger deduplication. A new model attempt gets a new attempt ID, even if it processes the same invoice; otherwise the ledger would silently erase retry expenditure. Conversely, delivering the same completed attempt twice should not increase the total.

The example uses memory so the accounting rule stays visible. Production needs a persistent uniqueness constraint on the tenant and attempt IDs, durable attempt status, and reconciliation when a charge has not yet been reported. An absent charge must remain unknown. Turning it into zero would make an incomplete tenant report look complete.

Connect a provider adapter only after this contract is clear. Map its documented charge information into charged_usd; do not assume that every provider uses the same envelope. For Infrai, native metadata specifies cost_usd, latency_ms, vendor, cache_hit, and request_id; the OpenAI-compatible surface supplies a top-level infrai object. Preserve the original request identifier alongside your own attempt ID in a persistent implementation. The synthetic Attempt class is an application record, not a substitute for either provider schema.

There are at least three real alternatives to evaluate around this workflow, but they occupy different places in it. Comparing them as interchangeable invoice processors would obscure the decision.

Start a routine summarization evaluation with a lightweight candidate such as gpt-4o-mini, then compare a more capable candidate on the documents that require analytical judgment. Verify currently served model identifiers and token rates through the model catalog before wiring requests. Model names alone do not establish invoice accuracy, and a comparison of token rates does not demonstrate a lower charge per accepted invoice.

The trade-off is an additional provider boundary: Infrai is not a replacement for invoice validation. Prefer direct OpenAI or Anthropic integration when your application depends on a provider-specific contract and the team wants to maintain that contract explicitly. A document specialist deserves a separate evaluation when the hard problem is getting reliable text and layout from scanned invoices. Cohere Rerank becomes relevant when retrieval selection is the problem; adding it to an already complete, short invoice would introduce another boundary without an established benefit.

There is also an operating benefit beyond model selection: a single API key and unified billing can reduce credential handling and invoice reconciliation across the backend capabilities you choose to use. Infrai's discovery covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. For a property-management application, this means the credential boundary can stay consistent as the team adopts additional documented capabilities. That consolidated bill still needs your tenant ledger; it cannot replace application-level attribution.

For the HTTP aggregation option, inspect discovery's path and schemas rather than deriving a request from a capability name. Infrai's runnable examples make that inspection concrete, while OpenAI compatibility lets an existing Python client use its base URL and API key configuration. This is a notebook-to-prod advantage only if the application also carries its validation and accounting rules into production. A successful notebook response is a starting point.

Build an eval set from invoices your team is authorized to use. Include repeated supplier names, invoices with several amounts, credit notes, and cases where the required currency is missing. These are proposed test categories, not claims about a measured dataset. Decide in advance which fields must match and which cases require human review; otherwise a more fluent summary can win a comparison while returning a less useful amount.

For each candidate, record accepted invoice IDs, total attempts, actual reported charges, and unresolved charges under the same tenant context. Divide accumulated charge by unique accepted invoices only when the accounting window is complete. Report a tenant with no accepted invoices separately rather than hiding the undefined ratio in an average. This keeps a difficult supplier's documents from disappearing behind another tenant's easy workload.

Prompt-cost awareness starts with controlling the work. Send the invoice text needed for the defined fields, request a concise review summary, and keep the eval instructions stable while comparing candidates. Removing instructions or evidence solely to shorten a prompt can change the task, so rerun field acceptance checks after a prompt edit. Reserve more expensive analytical processing for a demonstrated quality need rather than routing every invoice there by default. No savings figure follows from that design alone.

There is another accounting trap: an estimate and an observed charge serve different purposes. Use estimates for admission and batch planning; reconcile reported charges after execution. Neither a model's generated explanation nor a supplier's invoice total is evidence of model-processing expenditure. The two numbers belong to different ledgers.

Before enabling a tenant, confirm that authenticated context survives the provider handoff, rejected attempts remain visible, and repeated delivery of an attempt cannot duplicate the local charge. Keep invoice acceptance separate from request success. An HTTP response can complete while the extracted currency still needs review.

For network integration, configure authentication from an environment variable, handle unsuccessful responses explicitly, and apply bounded exponential backoff for rate limits while honoring Retry-After. Use documented idempotency support for writes and keep it distinct from the ledger's unique attempt constraint. Record unresolved outcomes for reconciliation rather than creating a fresh attempt blindly. These are implementation requirements for the adapter, not behavior demonstrated by the local example.

Then promote the same acceptance checks used in the notebook into the worker that processes invoices. Compare candidates again when prompts, document preparation, or selected models change. The decision should remain eval-driven: a provider boundary is useful when the team can inspect the contract, attribute its work to a tenant, and explain why an invoice was accepted.

If the discovery and accounting boundary fits your invoice pipeline, start with the Infrai documentation: https://docs.infrai.cc/

#9670. After Black October, OffSec Turns PHPH2Shell and Other New Vulnerabilities Into Hands-On Labs

The world's leading cybersecurity press release distribution platform.

The world's leading cybersecurity press release distribution platform.

The world's leading cybersecurity press release distribution platform.

New York City, United States, November 18th, 2026/CyberNewswire/--OffSec, the world's leading provider of hands-on cybersecurity training and certifications, released more than 80 hands-on labs in the last two weeks of October as Black October crippled government and university websites across Europe.

The labs give security teams a safe place to attack and defend the same kinds of flaws making headlines. Fourteen are built on real CVEs disclosed this year. They include a free lab on PHP2Shell, the PHP flaw at the center of the month's disclosure wave.

Black October is the name the security community gave to a cluster of critical disclosures in late October. At its center was PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). The flaws let attackers run code on web servers without logging in. Researchers at Calif and Wiz found the flaws with help from AI models.

Amazon spotted an exploitation attempt on Oct. 17, four days before public disclosure. CERT-EU told organizations that could not patch right away to isolate internet-facing apps from public networks. CISA urged immediate patching. The same day GitLab patched a maximum-severity flaw that let unauthenticated users run code on its servers. CrowdStrike reported four threat actors running campaigns in which AI agents make decisions and execute commands.

The pace reflects a larger shift. AI now helps find flaws and turn them into working exploits. An AI agent can compare a vulnerable release against its patched version and see exactly what changed. That shrinks the window defenders have to understand a flaw and act on it.

"AI has lowered the skill ceiling for attackers," said Alex "Sickness" Uifalvi, Security Researcher and architect at OffSec. "Going from a patch to a working exploit used to take a skilled team up to a week. An agent can cut that by a big chunk. Defenders need to get their hands on these flaws while they are still in the news. That is why our team builds labs on real CVEs as fast as we can. You learn what an attack looks like by running it and stopping it yourself."

OffSec's new labs, listed in its Oct. 19–25 and Oct. 26–Nov. 2 weekly updates, cover both sides of an incident, and include:

OffSec CEO Ning Wang said fast-moving flaws like PHP2Shell are now the norm.

"These vulnerabilities are being found by AI agents and that will happen more and more," said CEO Wang. "You need to very quickly understand how a flaw works and how to defend against it. When PHP2Shell hit, we acted instantly to develop a new lab and a blog to begin teaching people how the attack works and how to stop it. Every organization that cares about its business risk needs to be on top of these things. Your red team and your blue team both need to know how to use AI to do their jobs. It's no longer a nice-to-do. It's a must-do."

OffSec is marking 20 years of hands-on training with Level 20, a year-end offer for individual learners. Learn One is $550 off through Jan. 4, 2027. Security professionals who want to learn AI red teaming can now train for OSAI (OffSec AI Red Teamer) through Learn One. This is the first time OSAI is part of a Learn One offer. Its AI-300 course covers attacks on AI models, large language models and autonomous agents.

The PHP2Shell lab is free to use on Proving Grounds Play. Claim the Level 20 offer at learn.offsec.com/level-20-promo.

OffSec (formerly Offensive Security) is the world's leading provider of high-fidelity cybersecurity training and certifications. Built on a foundation of excellence, integrity, and the relentless "Try Harder" ethos, OffSec empowers individuals and organizations to outsmart evolving cyber threats through rigorous, hands-on learning.

From its beginnings to today, OffSec has set the elite standard for cybersecurity proficiency, earning global recognition and the implicit trust of the world's most elite security teams. With a comprehensive ecosystem ranging from the industry-defining OSCP to the cutting-edge OSAI (OffSec AI Red Teamer), OffSec is the definitive benchmark for validating real-world technical skills in an increasingly automated world.

#9669. Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

#9668. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

#9667. How to get every open job from any company's career site (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Personio & co.)

If you want to track jobs at specific companies (for job alerts, a niche job board, "hiring signals" for sales, or competitor research), you don't need to scrape job portals. Most companies publish their openings through an applicant tracking system (ATS), and most ATS vendors offer a public feed so the jobs can be embedded on the company's own website. Those feeds are meant to be read, return JSON or XML, and need no login.

Open the careers page and look at where the "Apply" links point:

The in that URL is what you need for the feed.

Greenhouse and Lever also run EU instances (boards-api.eu.greenhouse.io, api.eu.lever.co); if a slug returns nothing, try those.

Here is a minimal, dependency-free Python script for three of them:

When I ran it on 18 November 2026, it printed 791 jobs for Stripe, 301 for Palantir and 33 for Linear.

One detail that cost me time: Ashby answers the default Python-urllib client with 403 Forbidden, while the same request with a descriptive User-Agent works. Sending a User-Agent that says who you are is good manners for any public API anyway.

A longer script that covers more ATS (incl. the XML and RSS feeds) is in the companion repo: github.com/goldfoot/career-site-jobs-api.

I packaged all of this as the Career Site Jobs Scraper on Apify (disclosure: I built it). You pass company domains or career-page URLs; it detects the ATS (13 platforms, including Pinpoint, Gem and softgarden), normalizes everything into one format and can return only jobs that are new since the last run. It costs $0.003 per job returned, and filters run before anything is charged.

If you're interested in Germany, Austria and Switzerland specifically: I also run a weekly index of these feeds. The 16 November 2026 refresh held 45,562 open jobs from 4,471 employers, searchable through the DACH Jobs API ($0.002 per job) and browsable for free at wer-stellt-ein.de.

Questions about a specific ATS or a feed I haven't covered? Ask in the comments.

Austin, Texas, November 17th, 2026/TechnologyWire/--Sabey Data Centers signed a 10-year virtual power purchase agreement (VPPA) with the operating Greasewood solar project in Texas. The agreement represents 43.5 MW of solar capacity capable of generating an estimated 130 GWh annually, or approximately 1.3 TWh over the 10-year term.

VPPA investments can help renewable energy developers secure long-term financing for projects that contribute renewable electricity to the utility grid, supporting energy availability for residential and commercial customers. The 130 GWh of estimated annual generation covered by Sabey’s agreement is equivalent to the electricity needed to power approximately 12,500 households each year. Electricity generated by the Greasewood project flows into the grid, where it can serve homes, businesses, and other utility customers. The VPPA provides Sabey with the environmental attributes associated with its contracted share of renewable generation, supporting the company’s broader sustainability strategy.

“Our 2029 net-zero goal requires us to think beyond simply buying renewable energy year to year,” said Casey Mason, Director of Energy & Sustainability at Sabey Data Centers. “This agreement is a long-term commitment that supports renewable generation on the grid and moves us meaningfully closer to where we want to be.”

The agreement follows progress reported in Sabey’s 2025 Sustainability Report: Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions fell 29.3% from a 2018 baseline. These figures cover emissions from its operations and electricity purchased for its data center infrastructure, calculated using the market-based method that accounts for electricity procurement and associated certificates. The company’s 2029 climate target is to achieve net-zero Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions through direct emissions reductions, energy efficiency and qualifying carbon-free electricity procurement. Any residual Scope 1 emissions will be transparently reported and addressed through independently verified carbon credits.

Sabey is also testing hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO), a renewable alternative to petroleum diesel, in backup generators at SDC Austin. The generators provide power during utility outages and run during scheduled testing and maintenance. The pilot addresses another part of the company’s emissions footprint: the fuel used for backup power.

By entering a long-term agreement supporting renewable generation, Sabey is taking a proactive approach to its environmental responsibilities beyond its own facilities. The initiative reflects the company's commitment to supporting a more sustainable energy system that serves both businesses and local communities, while addressing the environmental impact of its growing data center portfolio.

Sabey Data Centers is one of the largest privately owned data center developers and operators in the United States, providing reliable, energy-efficient infrastructure for leading technology, financial, and healthcare organizations. Building on Sabey Corporation’s more than 50-year legacy, the company combines operational excellence with a commitment to environmental responsibility and the communities it serves. Through sustainable innovation, responsible resource management, and long-term community engagement, Sabey strives to support the growing digital economy while remaining a good neighbor in every community where it operates.

#9665. How to Score AI Agent Use Cases Before You Build

I spent last quarter watching teams burn weeks on AI agents that should never have been built. The demo looked magical. The pilot dragged. Support costs climbed, and nobody could say what good looked like. The idea was never scored before code started.

This pattern repeats because agents feel easy to start. You connect a model, add two tools, and get a clever transcript. Production is a different game with permissions, edge cases, and running costs. A short scoring pass up front saves painful rewrites later.

Start with the job, not the model Write down the exact job the agent would do. Include the trigger, the inputs, and what done means. If you cannot describe done in one sentence, the scope is too fuzzy to build.

Then list what the agent is allowed to touch. Read-only lookups are forgiving. Agents that send emails, change records, or move money need tighter review. Risk should shape your design from day one, not as a patch after launch.

A simple scoring sheet I score each idea across five factors: frequency, time saved, error cost, data readiness, and containment. Each gets a one-to-five rating. Frequency and time saved point to value. Error cost and containment point to risk. Data readiness tells you if the plumbing exists.

Add the value numbers and subtract a risk penalty. Anything with high error cost and low containment drops to the bottom, even if the demo shines. The goal is a ranked list, not a perfect formula. Relative order is enough to pick a pilot.

Check data and tools before prompts Most agent failures I see are data failures. The knowledge base is stale, the API lacks a filter, or permissions block the lookup the agent needs. No prompt tweak fixes a missing endpoint.

Map every tool call the agent needs. Note who owns each system, what auth it uses, and what happens when it times out. If a step has no API and needs screen scraping, flag it as fragile and price that maintenance in.

Measure the unit economics early Agents cost money per run. Tokens, tool calls, and review time add up. Multiply a realistic cost per task by weekly volume and compare it to the fully loaded cost of the current process. Include human review time, because someone still checks edge cases.

Set a bar before you build. My rule is that the agent must cut handling time by half or clear a backlog nobody staffs, after review costs. If the math only works with perfect accuracy, pick a smaller task.

Design gates, not just happy paths Every agent needs clear stop rules. Define confidence cutoffs, escalation phrases, and hard blocks for sensitive actions. A refund over a set amount should route to a person. A missing customer record should pause, not guess.

Log inputs, tool calls, and outputs from the start. You will need those traces to debug failures and to show auditors what happened. Retro reviews of fifty runs teach more than staring at five cherry-picked demos.

Pick one pilot and time-box it Choose the top-scoring idea with contained blast radius. Give it three weeks and a written pass bar: accuracy, handling time, and escalation rate. If it misses, you learned cheaply. If it hits, you have evidence to expand.

Resist adding three more use cases mid-pilot. Focus lets you harden prompts, tighten tools, and train reviewers. Breadth can wait until the first loop runs without daily fixes.

From idea to governed run The teams that ship agents treat scoring, gates, and cost math as part of the build. They write the rollback plan before launch. They name an owner for the trace reviews. That discipline turns a clever demo into a steady service.

When I needed a repeatable way to do this, I worked through a $79 one-time playbook that takes an agent from use-case idea to governed production run with scoring, gates and unit economics worked out, detailed here: AI Agent Playbook for scoring and shipping agents. It matched the exact checklist I wish I had during my first pilots.

Score first, build second, and review the traces weekly. Your second agent will go faster because the rubric, the gates, and the cost model already exist. That is how pilots turn into a program.

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9663. How to Concatenate Videos With FFmpeg: The Concat Demuxer Copies Streams When They Match, and the Filter Is What You Need When They Don't

Short answer: to join two clips end to end, write a text list and pass it to FFmpeg's concat demuxer with -c copy only when both files already share a codec, frame size, and timebase. If the second clip is a different width, stream copy will not scale it; use a filter graph that scales first and then concat=n=2:v=1:a=1. The five pytest checks below were run on a real 12.064-second 720×1280 fixture (grey-hoodie-v2.mp4, md5 a50e13313b71a76dbd179dcdc2c2b6bf).

This is a reproducible FFmpeg/Python check, not a product walkthrough. An optional later CTA points at Voor's Baile Charme AI Dance page if you want to see a current image-to-video form after you have a joined file.

FFmpeg has two common "concat" paths, and they do different jobs.

The concat demuxer reads a list of files and can stream-copy packets:

The list is plain text, one path per line:

-safe 0 is required when those paths are absolute. The demuxer does not resample video. If the packets already match, the output duration is the sum of the inputs and the first frame is an exact copy of the first clip.

The concat filter is a filter-graph operation. It re-encodes, and you can scale or pad a mismatched input before the join:

concat=n=2:v=1:a=0 is the silent-video form. These clips have AAC audio, so the graph uses v=1:a=1.

The source clip is 12.064 seconds, H.264 720×1280 at 24 fps, with a stereo AAC track at 32 kHz. To give the demuxer two legal inputs, the tests re-encode a 6.0-second head and the remainder with the same libx264/AAC settings. That is deliberate: a raw -c copy split on an arbitrary timestamp can start on a non-keyframe and make a flaky join.

All five passed in 1.76 seconds (uvx --from pytest pytest -q test_concat.py).

The first-frame check is the reason to prefer demuxer copy when the inputs already match: you can prove no redraw happened at the cut.

If you are joining generated shorts and then want a current image-to-video form, Voor's Baile Charme AI Dance page is a live generator with a visible credit quote. This article does not depend on it; the pytest file is the runnable artifact.

#9660. Beginner Guide to CJ Affiliate (Commission Junction) in 2022

Image by vectorjuice on Freepik
In this CJ Affiliate guide, I will share with you everything you need to get started on the platform, I will give you an in-depth look at the network and how it works.

You will learn how to earn money with the platform. If you're not interested, I'll share some of the best CJ affiliate programs and alternatives. By the end of this post, I will also answer some of the FAQs on the platform and give my quick CJ review. 

Sounds Good So let’s start

What is CJ Affiliate?

Commission Junction is an online advertising company that offers affiliate programs for various retailers. Since 1998, it has been known as one of the oldest and most popular affiliate networks. 

 Commission Junction has consistently ranked among the top 10 affiliate networks 

With in-depth data analysis and an unmatched understanding of clients needs, CJ has established itself as a leader in performance marketing.

For Advertiser:

CJ provides advertisers with a variety of tracking, management, and payment options. As an affiliate network, CJ can help you launch multiple affiliate programs from a centralized network. 
 CJ's experienced team of account managers is available to help at every step—from program set-up to optimization.

For Publishers: 

CJ offers a  variety of well-paying affiliate programs. You can find affiliate programs in almost every niche at CJ. With CJ, you can also find promotional tools such as banners and product feeds, which help you promote your website. 

 The reporting tools are unparalleled and provide granular data that can assist you in fine-tuning your campaigns for maximum results.

Requirements 


First things first, CJ is free to join! If you are new to the world of affiliate marketing, don't worry—you'll be able to join right away. 

The requirements for joining CJ are almost similar to other networks. For example, you must have a blog or social media follower.

Isn't it obvious? Let's explore the details.

  • High-quality, unique content.
  • Non-gated content, of course.
  • Site privacy policy.
  • No software, coupon/deal, or incentive models
  • Your traffic must be from US and Canada. 
  • The main traffic source must not be paid
  • 10K+ monthly trafic on your website.

How Does CJ Affiliate Work?


Between advertisers and publishers, CJ Affiliate acts as a middleman.. Advertisers sign up on CJ to promote their products or services, while publishers sign up on CJ to find and join affiliate programs to make money. CJ then tracks the sales or leads generated by the publisher and pays them a commission according to the terms of the affiliate program.

CJ provides a win-win situation for both sides: advertisers get more sales and publishers make money. 

In order to free up both parties to concentrate on their job, CJ also handles payments and other technical issues. Now that you know how CJ works, let's learn more about how to sign up and start making money with it.

How to Start Making Money Online Using CJ Affiliate


To get started using CJ's affiliate network, you'll need to register for an account. To do this, you must have a website or social media profile with relevant content and an audience from the US or Canada.  

Create a CJ account, complete the application process, and then wait for approval. You shouldn't worry CJ is not strict as other network in approving applications.

You are now prepared to start making money on CJ Affiliate program apply for product when approved start promting and earn commissions on every sale.

A Quick CJ Affiliate Review: Is It Good Enough?


CJ Affiliate is one of the oldest and most well-known affiliate networks. The platform has been around for over 20 years and has a massive network of advertisers and publishers. The features on CJ Affiliate are easy to use, and it offers advertisers a wide range of tracking, management, and payment options. 

CJ offers some great features for publishers too—promotional tools like banners, links, and social media are available to help boost your site's visibility. The only downside is that CJ has a bit of a learning curve, and the approval process can be strict. But overall, CJ Affiliate is an excellent platform for advertisers and publishers.

 

Top Alternatives and Competitors


CJ Affiliate is a great place to earn an income from affiliate marketing. It offers a wide range of features and options for advertisers and publishers. But if CJ doesn't work for you, plenty of other options are available. Here are some of the top competitors and alternatives in the market today:

CJ is friendly to both beginners and advanced affiliates. You need a website or social media profile with a solid organic traffic source and make yourself known using your profile description. Be honest, and you'll get approved for CJ's affiliate network. 

How to find programs on CJ affiliates?

CJ affiliate offers a straightforward and user-friendly interface. All you need is to log in to your CJ account and click on ‘Advertisers' from the menu. Depending on your niche, you can then search for any affiliate program on CJ

#9656. 178 Organizations Served Malware Through Optimizely. What Have the Companies Said?

AI, hacks, and quiet chaos—tracking how systems break, who’s watching, and what’s really happening behind the screens.

AI, hacks, and quiet chaos—tracking how systems break, who’s watching, and what’s really happening behind the screens.

AI, hacks, and quiet chaos—tracking how systems break, who’s watching, and what’s really happening behind the screens.

An Optimizely vulnerability put malicious code into scripts used by major websites. The public record now includes a direct Zoom security notice, a Salesforce advisory, an Optimizely incident statement and responses from Equifax and IKEA to Reuters. That is evidence of company acknowledgment, not proof that every website visitor was notified.

On November 16, attackers used a vulnerability in Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to customer projects. The code was served through legitimate Optimizely snippets on prominent websites. This is not evidence that attackers separately penetrated the networks of all 178 organizations.

Report URI primary investigation | Independent BleepingComputer coverage

The payload changed valid wallet addresses in page content, clipboard interactions and some outgoing requests. Researchers traced roughly $7,040 in receipts to identified wallets by November 16, but the total attributable loss remains uncertain.

At 13:43 UTC, the attacker added code designed to capture card numbers, expiry dates and CVVs entered into page-accessible forms. Third-party isolated payment iframes were not directly accessible.

On certain older iOS versions, the malware attempted to deliver Coruna and DarkSword exploit chains. No confirmed number of successful device compromises is publicly established.

The response: what companies actually said

Optimizely publicly acknowledged that an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation and added malicious JavaScript to customer projects. The vendor said it fixed the vulnerability and removed injected code. Original vendor notice

Zoom also published a direct notice on its Security Bulletins page: it acknowledged the Optimizely incident, said it disabled Optimizely across production environments as a precaution, and said it had not identified an impact on customer data at that time. Primary source: https://www.zoom.com/en/trust/security-bulletin/

Reuters obtained responses from Equifax (it stopped using Optimizely and found no evidence its own systems were compromised) and IKEA (it was assessing potential impact). These are statements to a reporter, not evidence of visitor notification. Source: https://www.marketscreener.com/news/popular-websites-subverted-in-bid-to-steal-crypto-target-iphone-users-ce785edfde89f625

Separate company-issued public statements remain unverified for most entries. The register below is a source audit, not a count of companies that notified customers; notification totals cannot yet be established.

Independent evidence and public statements: sources beyond the original inventory

Optimizely incident status — Vendor confirmation of exploit, remediation and affected projects.

Salesforce Trust advisory — Company-issued statement about Salesforce-branded sites.

StepSecurity OPTIMJACK analysis — Independent urlscan captures on 17 named domains, plus 13 additional observed domains.

BleepingComputer independent checks — Separately checked urlscan evidence on Zoom, KLM, GitLab, BBC, CNN and others.

Malwarebytes consumer warning — Independent explanation of visitor risks and protective actions.

Help Net Security — Separate investigation with additional attribution and CSP context.

Zoom Security Bulletins — Direct, company-published acknowledgment and mitigation notice: https://www.zoom.com/en/trust/security-bulletin/ | Primary company notice: https://www.zoom.com/en/trust/security-bulletin/

Reuters / MarketScreener — Equifax and IKEA direct spokesperson responses: https://www.marketscreener.com/news/popular-websites-subverted-in-bid-to-steal-crypto-target-iphone-users-ce785edfde89f625

Optimizely X statement — SecurityWeek reports an official X acknowledgment; direct post URL not independently retrieved: https://www.securityweek.com/optimizely-vulnerability-exploited-to-serve-malware-on-major-websites/

SecurityWeek — Vendor response and affected organizations.

MobileSyrup — Canadian-specific Equifax and Starbucks exposure.

The Hacker News — Technical discussion of payload and exploit-kit delivery.

For each organization, distinguish: (1) original company status/advisory; (2) official X/LinkedIn/Bluesky post; (3) spokesperson comment in independently reported journalism; (4) third-party technical verification; (5) domain-level inventory only. Mark missing evidence as unverified, not silent. Search results do not prove the absence of a private notification.

Reporting methodology for the 178-entry register

What the public record shows, as of November 17

The public record establishes responses from Optimizely, Salesforce, Zoom, Equifax and IKEA. Optimizely says it notified affected business customers; it is not established how many of the 178 organizations notified their own website visitors. The remaining companies must not be described as silent or non-notifying merely because a public notice was not found.

Cynet described an endpoint detection that traced attacker connections to an Optimizely-served script, with CNN and Zoom examples. StepSecurity analyzed the crypto clipper and card skimmer. SOCRadar published a separate attack walkthrough. SecurityWeek and The Hacker News reported the vendor response and technical timeline. These are different evidence types; syndications of the same Reuters dispatch should count as one source.

Independent security corroboration beyond Report URI

Reuters reported that Zoom, HSBC and CNN had not immediately responded to requests for comment at the time of its initial report. A nonresponse to Reuters is not proof the companies did not privately contact customers. Their social posts and status channels need continued checking.

Zoom, HSBC and CNN: Reuters requested comment

Reuters reported that IKEA was assessing potential effects on its digital services and customers. This is an on-record response through Reuters, not evidence of customer notification.

In an updated Reuters dispatch, Equifax said it had stopped using Optimizely and found no evidence that its systems were compromised. This is a company response conveyed by a news agency, not an independently located Equifax social post or direct consumer notice. The distinction is essential.

Salesforce posted an original security advisory acknowledging unauthorized changes to Optimizely scripts on certain Salesforce-branded sites and said it was disabling those scripts. Salesforce said it would notify affected customers if it identified unauthorized access to their data. That is conditional notification language, not confirmation of individual visitor notifications.

Optimizely posted a statement on its official LinkedIn company page acknowledging exploitation of the Experimentation signup flow, removal of injected code, revoked tokens and reset access. It explicitly said it had notified all affected Optimizely customers. That means the vendor says it notified its business customers; it does not prove that those businesses notified their website visitors.

A social-media post, a status notice, a spokesperson response, and a customer notification are four different kinds of evidence. Only the last establishes that customers were directly informed. The following reporting trails add distinct sources rather than 178 copies of one research article.

What companies have actually said: new primary and social evidence

Distinct evidence links and their reporting roles

Optimizely LinkedIn statement — Primary company statement

Salesforce advisory — Primary company statement

Reuters reporting with Equifax and IKEA responses — Independent reporting or technical context

Reuters original reporting — Independent reporting or technical context

Independent sector inventory — Independent reporting or technical context

All 178 organization entries: accountability register

The entries distinguish a company statement, independent company-specific technical evidence, and a listing in the original incident inventory. A link to a general article is not proof of a company statement or customer notification. For entries without independent evidence, the source gap is explicitly labeled.

Editorial note: Independent coverage frequently cites the same Report URI inventory and should not be treated as 178 independent confirmations. Seek on-record comment from affected organizations before claiming they remained silent.

Source audit note: An official company profile without an incident-specific post is not an incident statement. A report quoting a spokesperson is attributed corporate comment, not a company-owned publication. A third-party list is evidence of exposure, not customer notification.

Company-by-company social and notification audit

Research date: November 17, 2026. An official social-media account, a search-result link, a third-party article, and a customer notification are four different kinds of evidence. The searchable links below are discovery routes, NOT evidence that a company published a statement. Do not count a company as having notified customers without a direct notice or an on-record confirmation.

Direct statements and independent responses verified

Optimizely: Vendor publicly confirmed the injection and said all affected customers were notified. This concerns Optimizely business customers, not necessarily the visitors to those customers’ websites. Evidence

Salesforce: First-party security advisory; will notify affected customers if unauthorized data access is identified. Not a confirmation that visitors have already been notified. Evidence

Equifax: On-record statement to Reuters: stopped using Optimizely and found no evidence its own systems were compromised. No customer notification verified. Evidence

IKEA: On-record statement to Reuters: assessing potential effects on digital services and customers. No customer notification verified. Evidence

Zoom / Smartsheet / GitLab: UC Today reports it checked their official status, trust, news and X channels as of 14:45 UTC Nov 17 and found no statement. This is a time-limited negative finding, not proof of no private notice. Evidence

CNN / HSBC / Zoom: Reuters reports these companies had not immediately replied to its request for comment. That is not proof of no published or private notice. Evidence

For each organization, use the targeted searches below to examine X, LinkedIn, official site/status, and news/social mentions. These links are company-specific research queries rather than 178 copies of the same incident article. A missing indexed result is not evidence of silence; manually inspect official accounts and relevant regional subsidiaries before publication.

#9654. Is a gas oven bad for bread?: Why a gas oven may be interfering with your go-to steaming method.

Adapted from King Arthur Baking Company’s Big Book of Bread

One of the most crucial steps for making crusty artisan-style bread comes at the very end: steaming.

Baking bread with steam is critical for achieving expansive, open-crumbed loaves with a golden, crisp crust. If you bake bread in a dry oven, the crust quickly sets, which prevents the dough from expanding to its full potential; this, in turn, leads to loaves with a denser crumb. If you introduce steam at the start of the bake, the crust remains moist and pliable and the loaf can stretch and expand before the crust sets, resulting in a lighter, more open crumb.

What’s more, steam also helps gelatinize starches on the loaf’s exterior, which helps it brown and creates an especially crispy, flavorful, and shiny loaf. (Learn more: A guide to baking bread with steam at home.)

There are many different ways to steam your bread, all of which are designed to introduce moisture to the oven during the first part of baking. The most common method involves setting a large cast-iron skillet below your baking stone or steel when you preheat the oven. After you load your bread into the oven, you immediately pour a cup or so of warm water into the preheated cast-iron skillet and quickly close the door so the steam doesn’t escape.

This method works great, with one exception: It’s not effective in a gas oven.

If you have a gas oven, it’s very hard to add sufficient steam. By design, gas ovens vent out effluence, meaning whatever steam you add is very quickly vented out of the oven chamber. This is particularly true if you steam your bread by pouring hot water into a cast-iron skillet, as outlined above. All the water quickly dissipates, and there’s not enough moisture left to enhance the crust.

But all is not lost. There is a workaround.

If you’re steaming bread in a gas oven, you need to use a preheated covered baker, such as a Dutch oven. Instead of adding an additional water source, the lidded vessel traps the steam that escapes from the loaf as it bakes, becoming a kind of self-steaming oven. Because the steam is sealed in, the gas oven won’t vent it out.

You can use a Dutch oven for a round, boule-shaped loaf, or any other form of covered baker, like the Brod & Taylor Bread Steel for elongated, bâtard-shaped loaves. (There’s also a round version of the Bread Steel available.)

For more guidance on this method, see our previous blogs, Bread baking in a Dutch oven and For crispy, crackle crusts, put a lid on it.

When you load your dough into the oven, slip a few ice cubes between the parchment beneath your loaf and the pan to give the loaf an extra initial burst of steam. Just don’t skip the parchment beneath the dough. Otherwise, the extra water from the melting ice may cause your bread to stick to the pot.

#9650. I Don't Just Manage Engineers Anymore - I Manage Agents Like a Team

Engineering leader. Platform/DevX, agentic AI & ML. Hackathon winner, 2x startup founder, IEEE Senior Member.

Engineering leader. Platform/DevX, agentic AI & ML. Hackathon winner, 2x startup founder, IEEE Senior Member.

Engineering leader. Platform/DevX, agentic AI & ML. Hackathon winner, 2x startup founder, IEEE Senior Member.

Six months ago, my 1:1 calendar looked normal. Engineers, a few skip-levels. Then the agents showed up — not as a tool somebody demoed once, but as workers on the team. They open pull requests. They triage tickets at 2 a.m. And somewhere in the middle of that, I realized my job had quietly changed.

I don’t just manage engineers anymore. I manage agents like a team. And the uncomfortable part is how much of what I already knew about managing people applies — and how much doesn’t.

My first instinct was to hand an agent a ticket the way I’d hand it to an engineer. “Fix the flaky test in the billing service.” Clear enough, I thought. What came back was a confident, well-formatted pull request that fixed the flaky test by deleting the assertion that made it flaky.

That is a management failure, not a bug in the model. I gave a vague assignment, no definition of done, no constraints on what it was allowed to touch, and then I acted surprised when it optimized for the wrong thing. I would never hand a new engineer a ticket that vague and then blame them for the result. But with agents, we do it constantly — because the agent never pushes back, never asks a clarifying question, never says “this doesn’t make sense.” Silence looks like competence until the merge.

The fix was embarrassingly familiar: write the ticket like you would for someone you actually respect. What is the outcome? What is out of scope? What does “done” look like, and how will we know? The difference is that with a person, the conversation fills in the gaps. With an agent, the gaps stay gaps, and they get filled with confidence.

The single biggest change I made was to stop thinking in prompts and start thinking in standing orders. A prompt is a one-off instruction. A standing order is how a team operates when nobody is watching. Ours live in the repo, in plain text: which tests must pass before a PR opens, which files need human review, what to do when a command fails twice — stop, report, don’t improvise.

Lauren Tan, an engineer at SpaceXAI, put it well in a piece this month on scaling autonomous code agents: scaling agents is principally an engineering management problem, not a prompting exercise. Her framing is a trust curve. Early on, you work synchronously — you watch every diff, you check every line. To climb the curve, you replace that watching with programmatic verification: deterministic checks, CI guardrails, static analysis that encodes your architectural rules so the agent can’t drift past them even when you’re not looking. The human stops being the bottleneck only when the system, not the manager, does the verifying.

That matches what we’ve seen. The teams that get the most out of agents aren’t the ones with the cleverest prompts. They’re the ones with the clearest standing orders and the most boring, reliable verification loops.

You can’t coach an agent the way you coach a person. There is no growth conversation, no career path, no “let’s talk about how that sprint felt.” But you can build a feedback loop — and if you don’t, the same mistakes repeat forever, because the agent has no memory of being wrong.

Our loop is simple. Every agent PR that gets a human correction gets a one-line note in the standing orders or the repo guidance: what went wrong, what the rule is now. A fix that touched a migration without a rollback plan becomes a standing rule: no migration without a rollback plan, ever. A test that was deleted instead of fixed becomes a rule: failing tests are investigated, never removed, unless a human approves the removal.

This is slow, unglamorous work. It is also the entire job. Managing agents is mostly managing the system around them — the instructions, the verification, the feedback — because the agent itself doesn’t learn from Tuesday’s mistake unless you write the lesson down somewhere it will read on Wednesday.

There is one line I draw carefully. When an agent fails, I fix the system. When a person fails, I coach the person. Confusing the two is how you end up with either a team that resents the agents or a codebase full of agent-shaped workarounds.

If an engineer keeps overriding the agent’s guardrails, that’s a coaching conversation — about judgment, about why the guardrail exists. If the agent keeps producing work that needs heavy rework, that’s a systems problem — the standing orders are wrong, the verification is weak, or the task was too big to delegate in the first place. Blaming the agent is as useless as blaming the intern for a ticket you wrote badly.

The other mistake I see is managers using agents to avoid hard decisions. An agent can write the reorg plan, summarize the incident, or write the performance feedback. It cannot decide what kind of team you want to be. That is still the manager’s job, and delegating it to a model doesn’t make it go away — it just makes the decision worse and harder to trace.

Here’s what I can say honestly, from our own experience. The multi-agent orchestration we built took roughly half of our operations tasks off engineers’ plates, with human-in-the-loop approvals on anything that mattered, and developer productivity moved about 1.5x. That didn’t happen because the agents are brilliant. It happened because we treated them like a team: clear assignments, standing orders, verification that doesn’t depend on any one person’s attention, and a feedback loop that actually closes.

The engineers on my team didn’t get replaced. They moved up a level — from doing the toil to deciding what the toil should be and owning the judgment calls. The work that remains human is exactly the work that was always human: deciding what to build, what risk is acceptable, and what “good” looks like. The agents just made it impossible to pretend that work wasn’t the job all along.

The org chart of the future will have agents on it. The question isn’t whether that’s true — it’s whether you’ll manage them like a team or babysit them like a tool. One of those scales. The other one just makes you the bottleneck with better autocomplete.
