#9555. Evaporated vs. condensed milk: What's the difference? : Navigating the canned dairy aisle.

Navigating the dairy section at the grocery store is one thing, but when it comes to the canned stuff, how much do you know about the difference between evaporated milk and condensed milk?

Before we discuss what sets evaporated milk apart from condensed milk, it’s important to discuss their similarities. Evaporated milk and condensed milk are both concentrated liquids made from fresh milk that gets heat-treated until about 60% of the water content is removed. The primary difference between the two is the amount of sugar they contain and their resulting texture.

Evaporated milk will typically only contain lactose, or the naturally occurring sugars found in milk and dairy products. Condensed milk, on the other hand, contains around 40 to 45% added sugar. That contrast means condensed milk is much thicker (almost syrupy) and has a more pronounced sweet flavor (it’s no wonder it’s often referred to as sweetened condensed milk!), and evaporated milk runs watery in texture and is lighter in taste.

Because of the extreme differences in the sugar content and consistency, evaporated milk and condensed milk cannot be used interchangeably. There will be a very noticeable difference if you use evaporated milk in a recipe that was written to use condensed milk, or vice versa.

Using evaporated in a recipe that calls for condensed milk will result in a dessert that is too bland and watery, while using condensed milk in a recipe that calls for evaporated milk can make a dish way too sweet and thick. If your recipe calls for a very small amount (1 to 2 tablespoons) of condensed milk, you could get away with combining a spoonful of evaporated milk mixed with some sugar. But if your recipe needs one whole can of evaporated or condensed milk, be sure to use the correct type.

If you want to learn more about – and celebrate – the differences between evaporated and condensed milk, make this Tres Leches Cake, which is a fantastic recipe that utilizes the two milks with heavy cream in a luscious cake soak for dessert. For a different dose of double the milk, you’ll want to try this creamy, custardy Vanilla Bean Flan.

Evaporated milk provides richness and creaminess to dishes that are both sweet and savory. It’s often used to enrich custard-based pie fillings, like Hong Kong Egg Tarts, Delicata Squash Pie, and Pumpkin Pie. To round out your fall table and use up that can of evaporated milk, try the dairy ingredient in dinner recipes like Pumpkin Soup and Creamy Tomato Soup, or macaroni and cheese.

If you have an unopened can of condensed milk, you can also make dulce de leche with it. One way to go about it is to let it simmer in a pan filled with water for a few hours: Learn how to make it here.

#9554. Not Ribeye: Bobby Flay Recommends This Steak Cut For The Best Tacos

When taco night rolls around, you'll want to head to the butcher and grab some good meat. If you're making carne asada, your instinct might be to pick the ribeye. While it might be the gold standard of steak, tacos and ribeye are an inherent mismatch. Tacos are one of the most democratic foods out there, while ribeye is made for deep pockets and expensive tastes. Even Food Network's Bobby Flay recommends skipping it. Instead, he swaps the pricey cut for the seriously underrated skirt steak.

Ribeye is America's favorite steak thanks to its rich marbling and tender texture, but you'll rarely find it in taquerias. Beyond being pricey, ribeye's assets are its downfall in tacos. In an interview with Food and Wine, Flay revealed the reason why he often chooses to skip ribeye altogether: "[Ribeye] can be inconsistent because the fat doesn't always melt even when cooked properly." This is a real problem in tacos. Encased in a taco, you don't have the option to trim around a rubbery pocket of fat or leave it on the plate. Even if you trim the fat before adding the steak to your tacos, it's so unevenly distributed that you risk ending up with wildly inconsistent slices.

Unlike ribeye, skirt is cut from the plate primal, a hard-working area near the diaphragm. Rather than being streaked with generous ribbons of fat, it's comprised of long, coarse muscle fibers, which give it a chewier, more fibrous bite along with a bold, beef-forward flavor. Its thin profile may not win it fans at white tablecloth restaurants, but it's exactly why taquerias can't get enough of it. All that surface area compared to its thickness means skirt steak cooks quickly, soaks up marinades fast, and slices evenly, which is everything you want from taco meat.

There's no cut of beef more well-suited to carne asada than skirt. Literally translating to "grilled meat," the beef is usually marinated in a citrus and garlic blend, with the acidic ingredients helping to tenderize the surface of the meat. After being left to soak up the flavor for a couple of hours, it's then seared or grilled over an open flame or charcoal to impart a smoky, charred flavor (an air fryer also works if you can't grill). Because skirt is such a thin cut, it doesn't enjoy spending too much time over high heat; it only needs around two to four minutes per side. Skirt can be prone to drying out, so it would be wise to avoid cooking past a medium doneness.

How you cut skirt is just as important as how you cook it. Compared to other cuts, skirt has particularly long, dense muscle fibers, and if you slice them with the grain, you'll leave them intact, resulting in chewy, rubbery bites. Slicing against the grain shortens these fibers, turning them into more satisfying, bite-sized strands. To identify the grain, look closely at the surface of the meat to spot the direction of the muscle fibers running through the beef.

Although skirt is beloved by taquerias, that doesn't make it suited to all beef tacos. One popular style where we would skip skirt is birria, the slow-cooked, tender beef marinated in a chili-and-spice adobo served with a flavorful broth for dipping. The whole concept of birria revolves around slow-braising, requiring tough, collagen-rich cuts like chuck or beef cheek, which break down into tender, shreddable meat over several hours. While skirt does have some connective tissue, it's simply too thin and lean to survive hours of prolonged heat.

#9553. 128 graduation wishes and messages for every graduate

Graduation is so much more than a diploma. It’s often the beginning of a big, uncertain shift into the unknowns of adulthood, a new career, and a life that’s far less defined than it was when you were a student. For some grads, this shift is an exciting one. For others, it’s terrifying. And many feel both.

If someone you love is graduating, you may want to write them a message that honors this journey. You want your note to feel personal, thoughtful, and maybe even a little inspiring — but finding the right words isn’t always easy.

The good news is you don’t need to be poetic or profound to share a meaningful sentiment on your loved one’s special day. A simple, warm message that acknowledges the moment and the person is more than enough. Whether you’re writing to a high school senior, a college grad, or someone finishing their doctorate, we’ve pulled together graduation wishes that are thoughtful, grounded, and easy to make your own.

The best wishes are the ones that make the graduate feel seen and loved. You recognize all the effort they’ve put in and offer encouragement without adding expectations.

Here are four aspects of a great graduation wish:

It’s genuine: A heartfelt “I’m proud of you” means more than a forced life lesson.

It reflects your relationship: Speak the way you typically would with them. If you’re usually lighthearted, stay lighthearted. If you’re more heartfelt and earnest, go that route.

It acknowledges the transition: Graduation is a moment of change, which can be both exciting and uncertain. Acknowledging this can help bring relief to the graduate.

It avoids pressure: Avoid mapping out their future or telling them what’s next, as this can add pressure. Instead, aim for something like, “Whatever comes next, I believe you’ll succeed.”

Graduation cards can have a tendency to lean on phrases like “Wishing you all the best!” and “The future is yours!” On the surface level, these messages can be sweet, but they don’t always reflect the depth of the relationship you’ve built.

If you want the graduate in your life to feel seen by you, here are 72 wishes that can help you out.

Watching your child graduate may leave you feeling pretty emotional. Here are eight ways to honor their accomplishment and the person they’ve become:

Seeing you graduate makes me beam. I’m so proud of you.

Your hard work and determination have paid off big time. Let’s celebrate!

I’m so proud of the person you’ve become (and have always been).

This achievement is just the beginning. Can’t wait to see all that you do!

Every day you make us proud, but today especially. Congratulations!

Your journey has been inspiring. I’m honored to be your parent.

You graduated! Let’s celebrate this huge milestone. You earned it and then some.

Your future is bright, and I can’t wait to see it unfold.

Siblings often see the late-night essay writing and the quiet doubts their siblings experience. To reflect that, here are eight wishes that are both playful and heartfelt:

I’ve seen every late-night study session and all the hair-pulling that got you here. You earned this.

No one works harder than you, and look at what it led to. Congrats!

Watching you grow into yourself has been the best part of being your sibling. (Now, could you stop growing? You’re making me look bad.)

So proud to call you my sibling and even prouder to celebrate this with you.

You’re my favorite hustler. And you did it all without losing who you are. Congratulations!

Thanks for graduating so Mom and Dad can focus on you for a bit, and I can act out without them noticing.

Congratulations to the second-smartest kid in the family. (Just kidding!) I love you and I’m so proud of you.

I hope you’re taking a second to soak it all in. You deserve it. (Okay, that’s enough gushing. As your sibling, it’s my job to keep your ego in check!)

Your friends have seen you at your best and worst and everything in between. Here are eight ways to reflect that journey with warmth and honesty:

You finally graduated! Now, can we finally book a trip to celebrate in style?

You can get a full night’s rest now. Congratulations!

Hope you’re ready for me to be very obnoxious and introduce you as “doctor” from now on.

Start stretching now, because this is huge, and we’re going to dance until morning to celebrate it properly!

I’m lucky to call you a friend. Congratulations. I’m beyond proud.

You’re the hardest worker I know. Congrats. You deserve it!

Get ready to be embarrassed: Nobody is going to have a louder cheering section at graduation than you. Love you!

You’re so impressive, and I learn so much from you all the time. Congratulations, friend!

Related read: 44 questions to ask any friend to deepen your connection

If you’re a cousin, grandparent, aunt, or uncle, here are eight wishes that you can show support:

I’ve seen all the behind-the-scenes work that went into this moment. You’ve earned every bit of it.

You are so strong and resilient. I had no doubt this day would come. Congratulations!

You’ve grown into someone who leads with compassion and courage. It’s been a privilege to witness that.

Whether they’ve earned a PhD, MD, JD, or another credential, these grads have invested significant time, energy, and identity into their achievement. Here are eight ways to honor them and this huge milestone:

Good wishes for high school graduates should be grounded in encouragement. This is a time when everything feels new and a little uncertain. The best messages usually strike a balance between celebrating a significant achievement and acknowledging the emotional weight of leaving behind the familiar.

You might say something like: “You just accomplished something huge. Congratulations! And remember, it’s more than okay if the next step still feels a little uncertain.” This way, you’re honoring their hard work but also reminding them that they don’t need to have everything figured out yet.

Start by acknowledging the journey they’ve been on. College is typically full of academic pressure and personal growth. Let them know how proud you are of the person they’ve become.

You might say something like, “You’ve worked so hard, and I can’t wait to see what comes next. I’m so proud of the incredible person you are.”

Congratulate them, then add one kind thing about them. A few lines is plenty for a card. Here are some words for a graduation card, from short greetings to more personal notes:

"Congrats, grad! Your future is lucky to have you."

"Congratulations, graduate! I'm so proud of you."

"I've seen how much effort this took. I hope you feel so proud today."

"You kept going, even when things were hard. That says so much about who you are."

A good way to personalize a message is to reflect on what you admire about the graduate or how you’ve seen them evolve. Try naming something specific, like a moment they overcame something, or how they’ve impacted you.

Remember, you don’t need to write a long note. A short message like, “You’ve always led with compassion, and I admire that so much,” is powerful.

Funny graduation wishes are okay — just make sure the tone matches the moment. A light joke about student loans, caffeine dependency, or group projects gone wrong can land if it feels warm and comes from a place of love.

But as a rule of thumb, aim to avoid anything that pokes fun at their future or compares them to others.

A short message can still carry a lot of heart if it’s honest and specific. Here are a few examples that speak to a person’s strength and growth.

“You did it even when it felt impossible, and that says everything about how strong you are.”

“You poured your sweat and tears into this and earned every moment of it. I’m beyond proud.”

“I couldn’t be prouder of you and can’t wait to see what you do next.”

A good congratulations message for a graduate does two things. It says congratulations in plain words, and it names one thing you admire, like how hard they worked.

How you deliver it matters too. In person, a hug and “I’m so proud of you” mean a lot. In a card or text, you might write, “Congratulations on your graduation! I’ve loved watching you work toward this day.” Skip questions about what comes next. Many grads are still figuring that out, and today is for celebrating what they’ve done.

Start with congratulations, then add one thing you've loved watching her do. A line or two is plenty for a card. Here are short graduation messages for a granddaughter, whether she's finishing high school, college, or another program:

"So proud of you, my granddaughter. Congratulations on your graduation!"

"Watching you become who you are has been one of the great joys of my life. Congratulations, sweetheart."

"You're a very special young woman, and I'm so proud of all you've worked for. Congratulations!"

"You made it through high school, and I couldn't be prouder. Whatever comes next, you have my love."

"A college degree! Granddaughter, you've made me so proud. Congratulations."

"Being your grandma has been one of the best parts of my life. Congratulations, graduate!"

Congratulate the achievement and acknowledge the time it took. A doctorate often means years of research and writing, so mentioning that effort shows you see it. A line or two is enough. Here are a few short messages for a PhD or doctorate degree:

"Congratulations on completing your PhD. I've loved watching you work toward this day."

"You earned this doctorate through years of hard work. So proud of you!"

"Congratulations on your doctorate degree. I hope you take time to enjoy this one."

#9551. 19 non-traditional Thanksgiving desserts that aren't pie : Cakes, cookies, and even a tiramisu for your holiday dessert table.

Yes, Thanksgiving is a pie-centric holiday. But what if you don’t like pie? Or maybe you just don’t want it. Either way, we’ve got lots of non-pie Thanksgiving desserts, from spiced pumpkin cupcakes to sugary apple cobblers, plus plenty of autumnal cakes.

This adorable cake pulls double duty, serving as both a scene-stealing centerpiece and a feast-ending dessert. To make, stack two mini Bundt cakes together and frost with orange buttercream. Carving this frosted pumpkin at the end of the meal may just upstage the turkey!

Get the recipe: The Great Pumpkin Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Mini Bundt Pan Set

This dessert demonstrates how to dress up a crumb cake for fall: Top velvety sour cream cake with a juicy layer of apples, then crown the cake with a generous layer of apple pie-spiced streusel.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant Clearjel

Cranberry sauce can be a polarizing side dish, but everyone will love this New England-inspired cake, which pairs tart cranberries with walnuts and vanilla for a simple, satisfying dessert. (Because it’s so quick to make, this is a particularly good recipe for any last-minute holiday baking.)

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Sparkling Sugar

Sweet potatoes belong on the dessert table, and this recipe proves it. This ultra-soft cake is gently spiced and glows orange from the sweet potato purée, and it’s finished with a fluffy meringue that mimics marshmallow-topped sweet potato casseroles.

Get the recipe: Sweet Potato Sheet Cake with Marshmallow Frosting (make it gluten-free with Measure for Measure Flour)

To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9” x 13” pan

For a dessert that’s rich but not too sweet, turn to this recipe, which pairs pumpkin and pumpkin spice with chocolate chips. Baked in a decorative Bundt pan, it can be served unfrosted for an easy-yet-elegant dessert.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin-Chocolate Chip Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Soft Swirl Bundt Pan

Instead of apple pie, try an apple pan dowdy on your Thanksgiving dessert table. The pan dowdy is a traditional American dish from the 1800s and early 1900s. A combination of pie and pudding, the name comes from the method in which the recipe is completed: After an apple-based filling is baked in a crust-lined casserole, the baker takes a fork and "dowdies" the crust, breaking it into pieces that remain crisp despite being partially immersed in the juicy filling.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9" square pan

“Thanksgiving cheesecake” may not have quite the same ring as “Thanksgiving pie,” but when your guests are eating this ultra-creamy dessert, they won’t care. With its burnished top and custardy interior, this Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake reimagines the classic with bold autumnal flair, thanks to golden pumpkin purée and warm spices.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

Don’t be fooled by its stodgy name or humble appearance: This cake is so good, we named it our #1 best fall recipe! In fact, my colleague Jessica Battilana made it for Thanksgiving last year and declared it the biggest hit of the day; her guests fell in love with the moist, apple-loaded cake and fudgy brown sugar frosting.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Vermont Boiled Cider

If your biggest complaint about PSLs is that there's not enough coffee flavor, look to this Bundt cake, which has an espresso powder swirl running through the tender pumpkin crumb and a coffee glaze to finish the whole thing off.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Golden Wheat Flour

If you don’t want to fuss with pie, we suggest making a cobbler instead. This fruit-filled version pairs juicy spiced apples with a crackly brown sugar crust — both prep and serving are easy, and the resulting cobbler will absolutely steal the show.

Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon

Apples are great, but seasonal pears deserve some love too. This simple cake, made with a combination of almond and all-purpose flours, has a rich, buttery texture and an almost marzipan-like chew. Studded with fragrant cubes of ripe pear, it's an elegant after-dinner dessert.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Almond Flour

The boozy Bundt cake features potent maple flavor thanks to the 1/2 cup (!) of maple syrup in the batter, plus the sticky maple-and-rum glaze to finish. Made with cake flour and sour cream, the cake itself is dense and velvety, like all great pound cakes should be.

Get the recipe: Maple Pound Cake with Maple-Rum Glaze

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Vermont Maple Syrup and Natural Maple Flavor

Instead of slicing and serving dessert, bake every guest their own individual mini cake. Start with a moist, spicy sheet cake, then use a biscuit cutter or overturned glass to cut rounds for individual layer cakes sandwiched with cream cheese frosting.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Apple Pie Spice

Rich, silky, and balanced, this cheesecake is the kind of dessert that wins people (even cheesecake skeptics) over at first bite. Pecans are blended into the crust to add a subtle nutty flavor and delicate crunch. The ultra-creamy filling gets its sweetness from brown sugar and maple syrup, while heavy cream gives it an especially luxurious texture.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Maple Syrup

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Pumpkin Pie Spice

For a little French flair at your Thanksgiving table, make this classic tarte tatin. This dessert can be a little fussy, but we’ve endlessly tested our version to make sure it goes off without a hitch in your kitchen. And it’s worth it for the deeply caramelized apples layered over shattering pastry.

Get the recipe: Classic Apple Tarte Tatin

To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9” round cake pan

Tiramisu gets a fall-forward spin in this coffeeshop-inspired dessert. Just like a caramel macchiato combines espresso, steamed milk, and a generous caramel drizzle, this twist on classic tiramisu layers salted caramel sauce between espresso-soaked ladyfingers and mascarpone filling.

Get the recipe: Caramel Macchiato Tiramisu

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Espresso Powder

Make serving Thanksgiving dessert a breeze by baking up a big batch of cupcakes. These are packed with pumpkin flavor and spice, then finished with an easy swoop of cream cheese frosting. If you really want to level up your presentation, check out these cupcake decorating techniques for a pro-level finish.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Cupcakes (make them gluten-free with Measure for Measure Flour)

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Unbleached Cake Flour

This holiday-ready version of our five-star Everyday Olive Oil Cake is adorned with a big red bow in the form of a simple but stunning cranberry glaze. Made by cooking cranberries with orange juice, then whisking the mixture with confectioners’ sugar, the icing adds a bright tartness that complements the rich cake.

Get the recipe: Cranberry-Orange Olive Oil Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: King Arthur Square Pan

#9550. Add This Creamy Dip To Ground Beef For Juicier, More Flavorful Burgers

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

The perfect burger can be hard to come by. When you're going out, Food Republic's list of the best burgers in every state can be helpful, and there are even some great fast food options. But when you're looking for a super juicy and flavorful homemade grilled or pan-fried patty, what's the best route to take?

Sometimes, it all comes down to what you mix into the ground beef. While Bobby Flay uses only salt and pepper to season his patties, some folks swear by Worcestershire sauce and garlic powder for a kick of flavor. But there's one ingredient you may not have thought of that will keep your end result wonderfully succulent. Try mixing some onion dip into your ground beef. It's one of the clever ingredients that make burgers juicier, and it will add loads of flavor.

Onion dips generally come seasoned with dried onion and garlic, salt, and other herbs, plus a little sugar for sweetness. Add to that the sour cream base, and you have a rich, bold, slightly tangy, umami-filled burst of flavor that won't overpower your taste buds. And because you're mixing the dip directly into the beef before cooking, it can help keep your patties nice and moist (as long as you don't overcook them). Sour cream is simply cultured cream, so it has a high moisture content, and the added seasonings aren't so coarse that they will burn before the beef itself is cooked.

When it comes to what dip to use, classics like Dean's French Onion or Daisy Sour Cream French Onion, which is available on Amazon, will work great, but pretty much any brand will work. Depending on how much tangy flavor you want, you'll need about a half-cup to a full cup of dip per 2 pounds of beef.

The beauty of using onion dip in your burgers is that it's a one-ingredient solution, but you can increase the intensity with extra onion powder or fresh minced or dried onions. Just don't overdo it on the onion pieces, or the patties could fall apart on the grill. If you're going heavy on the amount of dip you use, you may want to think about adding some breadcrumbs as a binding agent. Dried parsley makes a great mix-in, as do other Italian herbs, but you should start sparingly so they don't overpower the flavor you're aiming for.

As for toppings, the regular stuff will do, but you might want to hold off on the ketchup and mustard until you've had a bite. Caramelized onions are an obvious choice, or you can give your burger some crunch with crispy fried onions. And you can always add an extra dollop of onion dip on top for more creamy flavor and texture.

Lastly, this trick will also work with a dried dip mix. Just mix it in with sour cream before you make the burgers. And if you want a similarly juicy bite without the added zing, try using mayonnaise in your burger. But for a juicy texture and plenty of zesty flavor, grab that onion dip out of the fridge.

#9549. Can Well-Being Give You Two More Years of Life?

Become a subscribing member today. Help us continue to bring “the science of a meaningful life” to you and to millions around the globe.

Greater Good Science Center • Magazine • In Action • In Education

Decades of scientific inquiry have found that the quality and length of a person’s life goes up when they experience less depression, anxiety, or other mental health conditions. More recent studies of psychological well-being—also referred to as happiness, flourishing, thriving, or the good life (among other terms)—have been reporting positive links to health and longevity.

For many, this combination of findings raises a question: “Does human mortality depend on the presence of human happiness and flourishing, or merely on the absence of mental health symptoms or bad feelings?”

That’s what Max Genecov and David S. Yeager explored in a recent meta-analysis, which combined findings from 99 different studies that measured mental health symptoms and conditions, well-being scores, and lifespan. Importantly, all the studies that they drew from used a longitudinal method, which means they took measurements repeatedly over time to explore whether momentary scores or score changes over time (e.g., well-being in early adulthood, or improvement in well-being) correspond with later scores or changes in another factor (such as the age or cause of death).

Well-being is generally understood as a combination of regularly feeling positive emotions, being satisfied with your life, and having a sense of meaning and purpose in life; ill-being reflects frequent and persistent negative emotions, chronic dissatisfaction, and purposelessness.

To get at this question of whether mental ill-being and well-being over time had overlapping, combined, or independent effects on all-cause mortality, Genecov and Yeager used a statistical approach that allowed them to correct for multiple factors under consideration. Their method was able to mathematically enumerate the impact of well-being on mortality while subtracting any coexisting impact of mental health challenges on mortality.

Why? Because if well-being and ill-being exist on a continuum, where reducing mental health conditions is ultimately the same as increasing well-being, then subtracting out the effects of ill-being would erase any concurrent benefit of higher well-being to mortality. But, if improving well-being and reducing ill-being independently affect mortality, where deteriorating mental health conditions and rising well-being contribute separately to how long a person lives, then their model would show distinct advantages of higher well-being to longevity above and beyond reducing symptoms of ill-being.

The result? In this study, people with higher-than-average well-being did live longer—and, indeed, this effect occurs above and beyond the lifespan advantages of lower-than-average ill-being. As the researchers sum up their results:

People one standard deviation above the average on well-being die at a 14% slower rate than those with average well-being. . . . As a practical reference using death probabilities from a 2020 United States Social Security Administration actuarial life table, a standard deviation increase on well-being corresponds to just under two years of more life for both men and women.

They saw older adults and patient populations with greater well-being live longer, and they also found people living longer who rated high in optimism, life satisfaction, positive emotion, a sense of social support, and purpose in life. This result isn’t new in the research, but by looking at the effects of ill-being, they were able to clarify its relationship to well-being and longevity. In fact, Genecov and Yeager found that the lifespan boost documented in their study (which controlled for the possible benefits of alleviating ill-being) was comparable to other studies of well-being and longevity that didn’t control for ill-being. This suggests that prior studies have also been capturing the unique and separate benefit of well-being to health and longevity.

While easy to grasp why, for example, less chronic stress would lead to better cardiovascular health and so a longer life, it’s not as clear from a scientific perspective why or how better overall well-being could help someone live longer. Right now, we know that optimism, positive emotion, social support, and purpose are associated with a longer life—we’re just not sure why, exactly.

That said, there are many ways mental well-being could fuel a longer and better life. More optimistic people, for example, tend to make healthier choices around physical exercise and diet, and to not smoke cigarettes. Positive emotions are linked to investing more effort toward and pursuing goals in life. People who score higher on measures of well-being are more socially appealing, generous, and compassionate toward others, and enjoy higher-quality friendships. One of the most famous studies of longevity attributes survival most strongly to supportive social bonds.

While still an emerging science, those findings suggest that well-being and related factors evoke experiences and motivate behaviors that measurably strengthen physical health in life-lengthening ways. While eliminating ill-being may diminish risks, obstacles, and barriers to physical health, fostering well-being may optimize physical systems to enhance stability, efficiency, and strength—both ultimately contributing to longevity but in different, often intersecting, ways.

Want to do more to enhance your well-being? The Greater Good Science Center has an entire website dedicated to supporting people who’d like to increase well-being called Greater Good in Action. You can explore and tinker with over 150 well-being–promoting activities, exercises, and practices drawn from published research, join a four-week Pathway to Happiness program, or try the seven-day Big JOY project.

Emiliana R. Simon-Thomas, Ph.D., is the science director of the Greater Good Science Center, where she directs the GGSC's research fellowship program and serves as a co-instructor of its Science of Happiness and Science of Happiness at Work online courses.

When manhood is an elusive, hard-earned status in a country, people there tend to be less happy and live shorter lives.

#9548. Who Makes Costco's Kirkland Signature Red Blend Wine?

Culinary mysteries span many topics, whether the origins of chicken à la king or the closely guarded composition of Coca-Cola. Yet one unknown that perpetually probes consumers is which producer is behind Costco's private-label alcohol. The Kirkland Signature labels conceal a treasure trove of well-priced bottles, spanning not only every major liquor style, but also a varied selection of wine and (formerly) beer.

A bottle label that commands special intrigue is the Kirkland Signature California Red Blend. This vino comes packaged in an eye-catching 1.5-liter bottle, all while sold for under $10. You'd think that such a size would make sleuthing the producer tricky. However, the brand behind this budget pick is listed directly on the bottle: DC Flynt MW Selections.  A large company responsible for both cellaring and bottling, this producer and distributor oversees a widespread U.S. and global portfolio, making it a natural match for Costco.

DC Flynt MW Selections is primarily headquartered in Louisiana, but the Kirkland Signature bottle lists the origin as Modesto, California. This suggests that at least some of the grapes are assembled in California's Central Valley region, as Modesto is only about two hours from Napa Valley — although precise vineyard sourcing is unknown. The same brand is also behind bottles from Sonoma, Napa, and Alexander Valley. Similarly, it produces Kirkland Signature's chardonnay as well.

As one of the least expensive Kirkland Signature wines, you might not expect an oenophile-appreciated experience with this bottle. Yet despite this accessible price point, the wine garners positive reviews: "A proof that [mass-marketed] wines can actually be good," noted Vivino reviewer Anton A., who gave the wine 4 stars. On the platform, the wine is rated 3.7 out of 5 stars, with over 3,500 reviews. Furthermore, other reviewers have given it favorable scores, praising the wine's balance of fruit-forward and spice flavors.

Typically, affordable California red blends are known for sweet "jammy" flavors, meaning the composition is heavy on sugar. Yet as noted right on the Kirkland label itself, this bottling strays from aggressive fruit-forwardness. Notes of oak and spice help contrast the fruit, a sentiment upheld by reviewers: "More [Bordeaux-like] than a California fruit bomb, but extremely tasty," noted another Vivino user — although some drinkers do take issue with its moderate palate. "[Not] flavorful enough, not jammy enough, not [oaky] enough," critiqued a Reddit user. Still, at a price point that even beats out affordable Trader Joe's picks, it's wine worth adding to a Costco shopping haul.

#9547. This Thanksgiving, make your pies mini: Mini pies may be the secret to a stress-free celebration.

What’s the one food you most look forward to at Thanksgiving?

For some it’s the turkey. For others it’s the array of sides. But for many of us bakers, let’s admit it — our thoughts skip right over the apps and main meal and go straight to the pies, whether it's apple, pumpkin, pecan, or all of them together.

The problem is that for smaller gatherings, the need for multiple pies diminishes. Still, how can you bear to choose between apple, pumpkin, and pecan?

Enter the mini pie, a great way to showcase an array of pies and have them all disappear by the end of the day.

Here’s a potential hosting scenario this year: You’re serving six close family members (including yourself) at Thanksgiving dinner; you want to offer pumpkin, apple, and pecan pie. So you pull out your mini muffin pan and use it to make mini pies in a variety of different flavors. Everyone can enjoy one mini pie immediately, one later, and squirrel one away for the next day.

And mini pies aren't just handy for smaller gatherings — they can also make life a little easier during the frenetic rush of food prep in the days before Turkey Day. Helpfully, you can make these pies well ahead of Thanksgiving; they can be prepared, baked, and then frozen for up to a few weeks before serving.

Once cool, wrap each pie individually in plastic, then bag them all airtight and freeze. When you’re ready to serve, unwrap, thaw, and reheat briefly: 5 to 10 minutes in a 350°F oven or about 20 seconds (per pie) in a microwave will bring them back to life.

Because these mini pies have a higher crust-to-filling ratio, you don't need to prebake the crust to avoid a soggy bottom. Just place the pie dough rounds in your mini muffin pan, fill with about a tablespoon of the pumpkin custard, and bake.

Another benefit: The smaller amount of filling makes it easier to nail the bake. You don't have to look for a perfect amount of jiggle in your pie before removing from the oven — just bake until the exposed edges are golden brown and the custard is set in the center.

Turn to our Pecan Tassies recipe — a beloved Southern dessert, pecan tassies are basically just bite-size pecan pies. This recipe uses a tender, unsweetened cream cheese pastry, which cradles a gooey nut filling sweetened with brown sugar (no corn syrup).

We’ve saved perhaps the most beloved pie for last: apple. These mini apple pies are a bit more involved than the pumpkin or pecan pies. You need to precook the filling, and you have to choose how to top them. That said, they’re totally worth the effort (and the filling can be prepared up to five days in advance; store the cooled filling, covered, in the refrigerator until ready to bake).

Once you've precooked the diced apple filling on the stovetop to remove excess liquid, assemble your pies in your mini muffin pan by lining with rounds of pie dough and adding the apples. You can then choose how to top them:

You may be questioning whether making mini Thanksgiving pies is more trouble than it's worth. But helpfully, the techniques involved are very approachable — mix, roll, fill, bake — and the resulting pies are both delicious and just plain fun. Have you ever wanted a whole Thanksgiving pie just for yourself? You can have it — in miniature. Happy baking!

Do you say you won't dare bake pie because you're unsure of your skills with a rolling pin? Check out these other easy no-roll crusts: No-Roll Pie Crust and Graham Cracker Crust.

#9546. How to stop emotional flooding from disrupting your relationships

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

The argument started with the dishes. Now you're saying something you know you’ll regret. Two minutes ago, you were mildly annoyed. Now your heart is pounding, and you can barely hear your partner over the noise in your own head.

This is emotional flooding, and it can happen to anyone. It isn’t a character flaw, and it doesn’t mean you're bad at relationships. When emotions run hot, the level-headed version of you can seem to vanish.

Flooding tends to show up when you're close to someone and the stakes feel personal. Fortunately, if you spot the signs early, you can keep an argument from turning into a blowup. Ahead, we’ll explore the science behind emotional flooding and how to calm yourself when it hits.

Emotional flooding is a state of overwhelm during a heated moment, usually a conflict. The term comes from John Gottman, PhD, who describes flooding as the point when you’re so overloaded that you can't take in new information, solve the problem, or hear the person in front of you.

Gottman and his colleague Robert Levenson studied couples at the University of Washington. As partners argued, they tracked physical signals like heart rate. Couples whose bodies showed higher arousal during conflict tended to grow less satisfied with their relationship over the following years.

Flooding feels different from person to person, so you may notice some of these signs but not others. Here's what to look for:

Racing heart: Your pulse climbs, and you feel your heartbeat in your chest or throat.

Fast, shallow breathing: Your breaths come quick and tight, and a full inhale feels out of reach.

Heat and tension: Your face flushes, and your jaw or shoulders tighten.

Tunnel vision: Your thinking narrows, and the other person’s words get hard to follow.

Urge to fight or flee: You want to raise your voice or leave, and it feels difficult to hold back.

Numbness or blankness: Your thoughts freeze, and you feel disconnected from the conversation.

Emotional flooding involves the amygdala, the part of your brain built to detect danger and keep you safe. When it senses a threat, it triggers the stress response and releases a surge of hormones that put your body on high alert. Adrenaline and norepinephrine speed up your heart rate and pull your focus toward the threat. That narrowed focus is part of why listening gets so hard.

In an everyday disagreement, there’s usually no physical danger, but your brain can still treat a raised voice or a difference of opinion as a threat, setting off the same alarm and the same rush of anger.

In close relationships, flooding may get extra fuel. Arguments can touch things that matter deeply to you, like feeling respected or safe. Old wounds and fear of where the fight might lead can pile on top of the present moment.

A note on relationships that don’t feel safe: This article is about everyday arguments, not abuse. If a raised voice or a pattern of control leaves you afraid of your partner, that fear isn’t a false alarm. Self-soothing isn’t the tool for this, and your safety comes first. You can reach the National Domestic Violence Hotline any time at 1-800-799-7233, or text START to 88788.

You can't always stop flooding before it starts, but you can help your body calm down once you realize it’s happening. Then, when you feel settled enough to think clearly again, you can gently return to the conversation. The tips below follow that order: calm your body first, then come back and repair. Try the ones that fit the moment, and skip any that don’t feel right for you.

The moment you notice your heart racing or your thoughts scrambling, tell yourself “this is flooding.” Naming it reminds you that the feeling is physical and temporary. That bit of awareness gives you room to choose your next move instead of reacting on autopilot.

💙 Try the Full Sensory Awareness meditation on the Calm app.

A longer exhale engages your parasympathetic nervous system, the part of your nervous system that helps you rest and settle down.

In one study, people who practiced cyclic sighing (also known as the physiological sigh), a breathing pattern of two quick inhales and one long exhale, reported bigger mood improvements than those who practiced mindfulness meditation.

If breathing exercises feel uncomfortable, skip ahead to the next tip.

💙 Press play on the Breathe to Calm Down session on Calm.

When you're flooded, stepping away can help you collect yourself before you talk things through. Tell your partner you need a break and that you’ll come back, so they don’t feel abandoned mid-conflict.

According to Gottman's research, it can take at least 20 minutes for your body to calm back down, so give yourself enough time. If you can’t leave the room, even a few minutes of silence can help.

Your body often responds to physical cues faster than logic. Use your time-out to splash cold water on your face or step outside for a few minutes of fresh air. Either one can help slow your heart rate.

💙 If anger is running hot, listen to Calm’s Investigating Anger session.

Flooding releases stress hormones that prepare your body for action. A brisk walk, or any gentle movement that suits you, gives that energy somewhere to go instead of letting it build.

💙 Explore Dr. Eric López's Walk Away Stress series on Calm.

Once it feels calmer, return to your partner. You don't have to solve everything right away. A short repair can open the door to trying again.

Try: “I got overwhelmed earlier. Can we try again?”

Gottman’s work suggests that how couples repair after conflict is a key predictor of long-term satisfaction, often more telling than how often they fight.

💙 Learn how couples meditation can strengthen your relationship.

Emotional flooding is feeling so overwhelmed during a conflict or another intense moment that you can’t think clearly or listen. The term comes from psychologist John Gottman's research on couples.

A common example of emotional flooding is a tense meeting with your boss, when your heart starts pounding and your mind goes blank. It can also happen at home, like when a conversation with a family member or partner escalates.

💙 Check out how to deal with a conflict at work.

Emotional flooding is a surge of intense emotion in a specific moment, while emotional dysregulation is ongoing difficulty managing emotions across a range of situations. Flooding can be one sign of dysregulation, but if it happens now and then, that doesn’t necessarily mean you have a pattern of dysregulation.

Emotional flooding can be more common and more intense for people with ADHD (attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder). Studies show that trouble managing emotions is a core part of ADHD in adults. With ADHD, you may flood more often or take longer to calm down.

If flooding feels constant or unmanageable, a doctor can help you figure out what’s behind it.

💙 Learn what ADHD shutdown is and how to manage it.

You can stop being emotionally flooded by giving your body time to settle before you continue the conversation. Take a break of at least 20 minutes, and try long exhales, cold water on your face, or a brisk walk. When you feel more grounded, give the conversation another try.

Mindfulness can help with emotional flooding because it trains you to notice early signs, such as a racing heart or a tight jaw, before they build. Over time, that gives you a chance to pause instead of react in hard moments.

Try to practice mindfulness when you’re calm, with short breathing exercises or guided meditation, so the skill is there when you need it.

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

#9545. Forget Mayo: Add This Creamy Ingredient To Tuna Salad (Hint: It's Egg Free)

Finding a delicious substitute for mayo in tuna salad can be a challenge, especially if you're looking for an egg-free alternative that's still creamy. But if you like a bit of garlic in yours, then toum — a Lebanese spread as rich in flavor as it is in fluffiness — is the answer you've been looking for.

Toum is a bit unique in that it relies on hefty amounts of garlic, oil, and vigorous blending to emulsify. Far lighter in texture than mayonnaise but not quite as airy as whipped cream, it's a perfect middle ground that imparts serious flavor to fish. While it won't have quite the same richness as mayonnaise, since it lacks eggs, this can actually work in your favor. It gives your final product a lighter flavor profile that's highly conducive to other simple ways to level up tuna salad, such as adding horseradish or capers. It's perfect for when you want a protein-laden lunch that doesn't feel too heavy and won't leave you in need of a nap.

Served cold, it's delicious. But when served warm in a tuna melt, the heat brings out the aromas of garlic in a way that's beyond anything else. The pungent notes fill your nostrils and blend with cheeses and toasted bread to create something as satisfying as any cheeseburger. Just be careful not to let any fall out, as toum's oil-based emulsion can separate or scorch when exposed to excessive heat.

If you like a denser tuna salad, one packed with hearty chunks and thick vegetables, then mixing in a dollop of toum and calling it a day works just fine. However, if you want something quite light and creamy, almost like a tonnato sauce, then you need some high-powered beating action. By adding the toum and tuna to a stand mixer or a bowl with an electric hand mixer, you shred the fish into fine pieces. This allows the fluffy nature of the garlic spread to almost suspend the protein, giving the illusion of increased volume without actually adding any additional ingredients.

Toum can be quite acidic depending on the brand and recipe, and the lemon juice can quickly work with any pickles or relish to make your tuna salad a bit overpowering. To avoid anything too intense, you may want to switch to sweeter varieties. Still, if you're a diehard believer in acidic additions, apples, hot honey (a true kitchen multitasker), or a pinch of sugar can all help balance acidity quite well and add little nuances of their own that work well with garlic.

#9543. How Couples Create Their Own Unique Microcultures

Do you have a pet name for your partner? I do, and many people I know do, too. Calling your loved one by a special nickname imbued with meaning—like “Bunny,” “Lumba,” or “Buncakes”—communicates in shorthand your unique connection and relational history. Using pet names is just one example of what some researchers refer to as “microculture”—a combination of shared language, rituals, stories, histories, and more that evolve between small groups of people in close relationships and help sustain them. Maya Rossignac-Milon of Barcelona’s IESE Business School and her research collaborators are looking into how microculture could play a role in the very smallest of groups, romantic couples, and whether it holds clues to how these relationships thrive over time.  “People experience this commonly, and our initial research suggests that it’s super pervasive,” says Rossignac-Milon. “We are basically proposing that attraction and, more importantly, relationship satisfaction is something that’s created together in the moment.” What microculture means for relationships While much relationship research focuses on how individual traits (like extraversion, emotional expressiveness, or attachment style) affect relationship dynamics, Rossignac-Milon and her colleagues suggest that the development of microculture also plays an important part in couple formation, happiness, and relationship satisfaction. “Two people can be quite different from each other, but, with microculture, they’re building something together that didn’t exist before their relationship, that’s totally unique to the two of them,” says Rossignac-Milon. “And it’s that process of cocreation that can be really powerful.” When people fall in love, they start merging their identities in certain ways and expanding their sense of self to include the other person. Creating a special microculture, consisting of inside jokes, pet names, repeated stories, and more, is one way couples cement their special connection. What does this look like in practice? Rossignac-Milon says there are three core factors that move everyday interactions into the realm of microculture: Mutuality: Something experienced and understood by both members—for example, a special word or phrase you use to signal that you need to talk, like “Let’s jaw.” Idiosyncrasy: Something unique to the two of you and not just part of a larger cultural system—for example, giving each other daisies instead of red roses on Valentine’s Day. Self-referentiality: Something that speaks to your relationship history and unique connection—for example, deciding “Because the Night” is “your song” because it was playing the first time you danced together. All three of these should be present for something to be part of your microculture. Consider this example. Every year, some friends of mine celebrate “the miracle of the tent,” a playful reference to the moment their platonic friendship turned unexpectedly romantic. Imbued with humor and meaning, this idiosyncratic holiday is part of their microculture, reinforcing their unique bond over time. Shared origin stories are a common way that couples create microculture, helping to sustain their relationship. When they reminisce about turning points in their relationship and share their story with others, it can increase relationship satisfaction, research suggests. Couples who initiate nostalgic recollections of past shared experiences feel closer to their partners and are more committed. Perhaps that’s why my husband Don and I like to prompt people to share their origin story when meeting them for the first time. (Not to mention, they often ask us to return the favor—a win-win!) Inside jokes can also express a couple’s microculture. For example, Don once bought me a t-shirt that he promised to wear with the words, “You’re right, dear,” printed on the front. I immediately got the joke—a humorous acknowledgment of times he’d insisted he was right about something when he wasn’t. Now it’s become a much-used catchphrase for admitting our mistakes. (He needs to say it more often than I do, of course). Relationship rituals can also be part of your unique microculture if they are symbolically meaningful (and not just routine). Bringing coffee to your wife in bed on a silver tray might be your tongue-in-cheek way of acknowledging that she’s not a morning person and needs princess pampering. Or eating at the same Italian restaurant the first Friday of every month might be a nod to how you fell in love there over a plate of spaghetti. These small rituals communicate shared history and meaning, helping couples feel part of something special. My colleague Katherine and her husband Brian developed a shorthand for recognizing moments when their dual-career family feels stretched thin. If either one needs to work late, instead of expressing frustration or being passive-aggressive, the other one says, “Thank you for doing that for our family.” This acknowledges that, while each of them would prefer to be relaxing with their kids and spouse, duty calls, and they’re doing the best they can to manage their work demands. The unexpectedly deep roots of microcultures Shared language, stories, and rituals are often the most visible aspects of microculture, says Rossignac-Milon. But, just like macrocultures, microcultures also involve a shared sense of identity, morality, and reality. Romantic partners tend to form identities as a couple that are distinct from their individual identities and serve to strengthen their relationship. For example, they may consider themselves to be “cat people” or a “power couple.” When partners are clear about their identity as a couple, it’s tied to higher levels of commitment. Having a shared moral code (shared values and norms) is also part of a couple’s microculture. This might include rules like never working on Sundays, requiring both people to apologize after a conflict, or being sexually exclusive on weekends only. If broken, these norms may elicit anger, hurt, or the need to repair; so, the extent to which they are agreed upon and easily managed strengthens a couple’s well-being. A shared sense of reality supports couples in their relationship, too. In a study run by Rossignac-Milon and her colleagues, they found that couples who perceive an overlap in how they view the world with their partner feel less uncertainty and more meaning in life than if they think their partner diverges from their worldview. When experiments manipulate a couple’s sense of agreement on their perceptions to signal disagreement, the researchers found, couples will try to compensate by leaning more heavily on shared microcultural references, as if to repair the rift in their shared reality. “People really care about this experience, and when it’s threatened, they want to protect their sense of, ‘No, we do have our own shared culture that we’ve developed together,’” says Rossignac-Milon. While aspects of microculture within couples have mostly been described theoretically by drawing on past research, Rossignac-Milon and her colleagues have begun to research the overall concept more empirically, too. In a currently unpublished study, she and her collaborators asked couples from diverse backgrounds to list three examples of each potential element of their microculture—from shared language to shared reality. Then, the couples kept daily diaries for two weeks, where they reported any references to their microculture that day and their feelings about their relationship. The researchers found that couples were happier with their relationship on days when their microculture was referenced more than usual. Also, looking at patterns across couples, those who referenced their microculture more were more satisfied with and committed to their relationship than those who referenced it less. “People who tend to have more microculture and use it more are happier in their relationships and are more connected to and committed to their partners across the board,” says Rossignac-Milon. The possible dark side of microculture Though microculture may help couples feel more connected and committed, there can be dark sides to the phenomenon, too, says Rossignac-Milon. Just like how some macrocultural norms and behaviors can make groups more insular or encourage shared false beliefs, microcultures can sometimes become problematic. For example, sharing perceptions or beliefs with your partner may increase your certainty in your viewpoint and boost your convictions, perhaps in a way that isolates you from others, says Rossignac-Milon. Similarly, you can sometimes reinforce unhealthy behaviors, like encouraging each other to smoke if you identify as a couple that smokes together, health risks be damned. A more extreme example might be how microculture can develop into a shared psychosis or support abusive relationships, says Rossignac-Milon. “If the rituals and norms that people establish together are toxic to begin with or have power dynamics that are fostering inequality and an asymmetry in the relationship, that can be dangerous,” she says. This suggests that couples should pay attention to any darker aspects of microculture that could have these nefarious effects. How to use microculture in a positive way On the plus side, knowing the importance of microculture in romantic relationships can help people make dating more productive, says Rossignac-Milon. Instead of just looking for “Mr. or Ms. Right”—someone who checks off your boxes in terms of traits you want in a partner—pay attention to what’s created between you when spending time together. That playful banter or those surprising connections are part of what makes people feel like they click. “Microculture is all about the experience of interacting and creating inside jokes and ways of using words that you have together and matter so much,” says Rossignac-Milon. “Letting yourself lean into that and using that as a diagnostic cue could be one important signal of compatibility that people are not always attending to.”  To encourage more of that special connection, she suggests taking small risks and not just saying what you think is expected of you. Those little idiosyncrasies or moments of vulnerability can serve to attract someone to you more than what’s on their resume. “Put yourself out there and use a funny word or do something that’s a little bit different from what others might do,” she suggests. “Those are the things that can easily turn into inside jokes and microculture that you can reference back to.” Couples in ongoing relationships can also benefit from paying attention to their microculture, she adds. It’s sometimes more natural to do that early on in a relationship and then neglect it over time. But continuing to reference your microculture and building on it is a way of keeping your relationship strong. “The more that people can keep growing their microculture, the more they can continue to reap those relational benefits,” says Rossignac-Milon. To nurture your microculture, it’s helpful to keep a spirit of joint creativity alive in your relationship and to introduce new experiences, inside jokes, rituals, and more. Otherwise, they can get old and stop having the same beneficial effect—similar to the way jokes can get stale and less funny over time, says Rossignac-Milon. On the other hand, there’s no need to put pressure on yourself, either, she says. Building rapport through microculture is something that anyone can do, regardless of who you are. “Jointly riffing, this kind of playful cocreation, may be something that some people are naturally good at, but it’s also a skill that can be developed by anyone, as long as they’re coming into it with spontaneity and a willingness to be a little bit vulnerable.”

#9542. This Vitamin Reduces Depression Symptoms By 50%

One vitamin reduced depression symptoms after a month, but the benefit depended on how participants felt at the start.

One vitamin reduced depression symptoms after a month, but the benefit depended on how participants felt at the start.

Taking a high dose of vitamin B6 for a month reduced depression symptoms in people already experiencing them.

The vitamin helps the brain produce chemical messengers involved in mood regulation.

The findings suggest a potential role for B6 in treating depression, although larger clinical trials are needed.

Almost 270 adults, mostly young women, took part in the research.

They were randomly assigned to take either 100 mg of vitamin B6, vitamin B12 or a placebo each day for around a month.

Among almost 60 people with at least mild depression symptoms at the start, those taking B6 improved more than those receiving B12 or a placebo.

Average depression scores fell by about 54 percent in the symptomatic B6 group, compared with 24 percent in the placebo group.

The benefit remained after accounting for differences in how severe their symptoms had been at the start.

The findings come from a new analysis of data collected in the same research programme that previously reported reduced anxiety after B6 supplementation.

Vitamin B6 supports several processes involved in regulating mood.

Dr David Field, the study’s first author, said:

“Vitamin B6 plays a crucial role in the production of several chemical messengers in the brain, including serotonin and GABA, both of which are central to mood regulation.”

GABA helps restrain nerve cell activity, contributing to the balance between excitation and inhibition in the brain.

Increasing B6 availability could boost their production, potentially explaining the improvement in depression symptoms.

Inflammation may also play a role, potentially affecting both depression and how the body uses B6.

Vitamin B6 occurs naturally in foods including poultry, fish, chickpeas, bananas and fortified cereals.

However, the trial tested a high supplement dose, rather than a change in everyday food intake.

High doses of B6 can cause peripheral nerve damage, so the researchers say supplementation at these doses requires medical supervision.

Larger trials now need to establish the most effective dose, monitor safety and determine whether B6 could help alongside existing depression treatments.

The study was published in the journal Depression and Anxiety (Field et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean
